keyConcepts: The value of a digit depends on its place. In 4,326, the digit 4 is worth 4,000 because it is in the thousands place. The digit 4 does not mean 4 ones here. 🟣 Interactive Model: Tap to Build 4,326 Build it, see it, write it.
lesson.missionQuestion: How does a digit get its value?
objectives: Identify the value of each digit in a four-digit number.
Build numbers with a place-value model.
Explain how the model and number form match.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: What You Just Saw Every trade kept the number exactly the same. That's because each place is worth 10 of the next smaller place: 1 thousand = 10 hundreds · 1 hundred = 10 tens · 1 ten = 10 ones When you trade 1 piece for 10 smaller pieces, the value doesn't change — only the grouping . That's what regrouping means. 4,326 = 4 thousands + 3 hundreds + 2 tens + 6 ones = 43 hundreds + 2 tens + 6 ones = 432 tens + 6 ones 📋 Same Number — Different Ways to Break It Apart Three ways to decompose 4,326. The total never changes.
lesson.missionQuestion: How many ways can you break apart a number?
objectives: Decompose a four-digit number in more than one way.
Trade place-value discs to regroup without changing the value.
Explain why two different decompositions can name the same number.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: What You Just Saw To compare two numbers, look at the place-value digits from left to right. Find the FIRST place where the two digits are different. The number with the bigger digit in that place is the greater number. You don't need to check the places after that — the comparison is already decided. 3,998 < 4,008 · 4,500 > 4,300 · 2,617 = 2,617 The open side of > or < always points to the greater number. Some students remember it as "the alligator eats the bigger one." 📋 Three Pairs, Three Reasons Each pair is decided at a different place.
objectives: Compare two whole numbers up to 10,000 using place value.
Use the symbols >, <, and = correctly.
Order a small set of numbers from least to greatest.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: What You Just Saw Reading a number line has two steps: Step 1. Read the labels at the ends. · Step 2. Count the spaces between ticks, then divide the total distance by that number of spaces. That's the increment . Once you know the increment, you can name any tick: just start at one of the labels and skip-count by the increment until you reach it. 4,000 to 5,000 with 5 spaces → 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200. So the ticks are 4,000 · 4,200 · 4,400 · 4,600 · 4,800 · 5,000. 📋 Three Number Lines, Three Increments Same rule. Different scales.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you find where a number lives on a number line?
objectives: Find the increment between tick marks on a number line.
Plot a four-digit number on a number line.
Read the value where an arrow points to a tick.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: What You Just Saw To find the rule of a pattern, compare any two numbers that are next to each other. The difference between them is the rule. If the second is bigger, the rule adds. If smaller, it subtracts. Once you know the rule, apply it to find the next number — or work backward to find an earlier one. 3,200 → 3,210 → 3,220 → 3,230 · Rule: +10 A pattern is just skip-counting with a rule. Find the rule, find the next number. 📋 Three Patterns, Three Rules Different rules. Same idea.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you find the rule of a number pattern?
objectives: Find the rule of a number pattern by comparing two numbers in a row.
Continue the pattern by applying the rule.
Use the rule to find a missing number in the middle of a pattern.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: What You Just Saw Every four-digit number sits between two thousands. 4,852 lives between 4,000 and 5,000. The midpoint between them is 4,500 . Below the midpoint → round down. · At the midpoint or above → round up. 4,200 is below 4,500 → rounds DOWN to 4,000. 4,852 is above 4,500 → rounds UP to 5,000. 4,500 is exactly at the midpoint → rounds UP to 5,000 (the standard rule). Shortcut: look at the hundreds digit. If it's less than 5, round down. If it's 5 or more, round up. 📋 Four Numbers, Four Rounds Notice the hundreds digit each time.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you decide which thousand a number is closest to?
objectives: Identify the midpoint between two thousands.
Round a four-digit number to the nearest thousand.
Explain why a number rounds up or down using the midpoint.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

items.title: Lesson 01.06: Rounding to the Nearest Thousand

keyConcepts: What You Just Saw The rounding rule is the same. Only two things change. 1. The rounding place shifts from thousands to hundreds . 2. The deciding digit shifts one place to the right — from hundreds to tens . Tens digit 0–4 → round down. · Tens digit 5–9 → round up. 4,820 has tens digit 2 → round down to 4,800. 4,872 has tens digit 7 → round up to 4,900. 4,850 has tens digit 5 → round up to 4,900 (midpoint). General rule: the deciding digit is always one place to the right of the rounding place. 📋 Four Numbers, Four Rounds Watch the tens digit.
lesson.missionQuestion: What changes when you round to a smaller place?
objectives: Find the midpoint between two consecutive hundreds.
Round a four-digit number to the nearest hundred.
Identify which digit decides the rounding direction.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

items.title: Lesson 01.07: Rounding to the Nearest Hundred

keyConcepts: The Pattern Is Now Complete Same rule, third (and finest) scale. Ones digit 0–4 → round down. · Ones digit 5–9 → round up. The unit's pattern in one sentence: The deciding digit is always one place to the right of where you're rounding. Nearest thousand → deciding digit is hundreds. Nearest hundred → deciding digit is tens. Nearest ten → deciding digit is ones. 📋 Four Numbers, Four Rounds Watch the ones digit.
lesson.missionQuestion: How precise can rounding get — and when do you stop?
objectives: Round a four-digit number to the nearest ten.
Round the same number three different ways (ten, hundred, thousand).
Choose which level of precision fits a real-world situation.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

items.title: Unit 1 Assessment: Numbers to 10,000

keyConcepts: What You Just Saw Four small steps, every time. 1. Break each number into tens + ones . · 2. Add the tens . · 3. Add the ones . · 4. Combine . You already know 4 + 2 (= 6) and 2 + 8 (= 10). The strategy just lets you USE those small facts to add 42 + 28. 📋 Three Quick Examples Same four steps, different numbers.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you add two numbers in your head?
objectives: Break apart two-digit numbers into tens and ones.
Add the tens, then the ones, then combine.
Use the strategy without writing anything down.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: What's the Same, What's New Same four steps as yesterday. 1. Break apart. · 2. Add the hundreds . · 3. Add the tens . · 4. Combine. The new wrinkle: When the tens add up to a hundred or more (like 90 + 50 = 140), that extra hundred just joins the hundreds when you combine. It's not a mistake — it's part of the answer. 📋 Three Quick Examples Same plan. Different numbers.
lesson.missionQuestion: Does the same strategy work for bigger numbers?
objectives: Break apart three-digit numbers into hundreds and tens.
Add the hundreds, then the tens, then combine.
Handle tens that add up to a hundred (the carry).

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: Subtraction asks: "How far apart are these two numbers?" Start at the small number. Count up. The total of your jumps is the difference. For numbers that are CLOSE together (like 30 − 27 or 90 − 88), count up one by one. For numbers that are FARTHER apart, use friendly jumps — to the next ten first, then by tens. 📋 Three Quick Examples Small jumps, big payoff.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you subtract in your head?
objectives: Count up from the small number to the big one.
Use friendly jumps to the next ten as stopping points.
Add the jumps to find the difference.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: To subtract a bigger number in your head: Break the second number into hundreds and tens. Subtract the hundreds first. Then subtract the tens. The hundreds part is easy. The tens part takes one more thought — but two easy steps is much faster than one giant step. 📋 Three Quick Examples Same recipe, different numbers.
objectives: Break apart the second number into hundreds and tens.
Subtract the hundreds first — that part is easy.
Subtract the tens next to finish the problem.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: To find a partner that makes 100 (or 1,000): Jump from the number to the next friendly ten (or hundred). Then jump to 100 (or 1,000). Add the jumps. It's the same count-up strategy from before — just with a round target. The pair you find is also the answer to "100 − that number" or "1,000 − that number." 📋 Three Quick Pairs Same recipe — two jumps.
objectives: Find the partner that pairs with a number to make 100.
Scale it up to find partners that pair to make 1,000.
Use the pattern to subtract from 100 or 1,000.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: When a number is close to a hundred: Round it up to the friendly hundred. Do the easy math. Then adjust by the small extra. For addition , you added too much — so subtract the extra. For subtraction , you took away too much — so add the extra back. 📋 Three Quick Examples Same recipe — addition and subtraction.
objectives: Spot numbers that are close to a hundred.
Round them up to the friendly hundred to make the math easier.
Adjust your answer by the small extra.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.lessonTitle: Strategies for Numbers Close to Hundreds

items.title: Lesson 02.06: Strategies for Numbers Close to Hundreds

keyConcepts: Every bar model holds three pieces of information: two parts and a whole. If you know both PARTS, ADD them to find the WHOLE. If you know the WHOLE and one PART, SUBTRACT to find the missing PART. The picture itself tells you which operation to use. Draw the bar before you start the math. 📋 Three Quick Examples Match the bar to the math.
objectives: Read a bar model — spot the parts and the whole.
Find the sum when both parts are known.
Find a missing part when the whole and one part are known.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.

keyConcepts: Four steps to solve a word problem: 1. Read it twice. 2. Find who's bigger. 3. Draw the bars. 4. Solve. The bar shows which number is the LONG one and which is the SHORT one. Once you see that, the operation is obvious — even if the words tried to trick you. 📋 Three Quick Stories Notice when "fewer/more" flips the operation.
objectives: Read a word problem carefully — twice.
Build a comparison bar model from the story.
Pick add or subtract based on the picture, not the words.

keyConcepts: Three habits of a good word-problem solver: 1. Cross out the extras. 2. Draw a bar (or sketch the picture). 3. Sense-check the answer. If the question asks for the BIGGER amount, your answer should be bigger than what you started with. If smaller, smaller. One quick look catches most mistakes. 📋 Three Quick Sense Checks What's the answer SUPPOSED to look like?
objectives: Find the useful numbers — and ignore the extra ones.
Spot the mistake in someone else's work.

keyConcepts: Two-step problems work in two stages: Step 1: Find the hidden middle number. Step 2: Use it to answer the real question. items.title: Unit 2 Assessment: Addition and Subtraction Part 1

keyConcepts: The column-addition recipe: 1. Stack the numbers — line up the ones. 2. Add right to left. 3. When a column adds to 10 or more, regroup the extra to the next column. The regrouped 1 isn't really "just a 1" — it's 10 ones bundled as 1 ten, or 10 tens bundled as 1 hundred. That's why it always lands one column to the left. 📋 Three Quick Examples Same recipe, different numbers.
objectives: Stack two numbers by lining up their place values.
Add one column at a time, from right to left.
Regroup when a column adds to 10 or more.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 3 math section

keyConcepts: The column-subtraction recipe: 1. Stack the numbers, top number on top. 2. Go right to left. 3. If the top digit is too small, UNBUNDLE 1 from the next column to the left. The total amount on the top NEVER changes when you unbundle. It just gets rewritten — like trading a $10 bill for ten $1 bills. Same money, smaller pieces. 📋 Three Quick Examples Spot where the unbundles happen.
lesson.missionQuestion: What if the top digit is too small?
objectives: Stack two numbers by lining up place values.
Unbundle 1 from the next column when the top digit is too small.
Subtract column by column, right to left.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.

keyConcepts: The cascade rule: Find the first NON-ZERO column to the left. Drop its digit by 1. Every zero between there and your starting column becomes a 9. The starting column gains 10. Setting Up Goblins in Canvas

How to connect each independent practice, concept check, and summative assessment to the correct Goblins student experience.

What teachers are responsible for

The Canvas course already provides three Goblins page templates. To minimize repeated work, customize each template once with your class information, save it as a master, and then duplicate that master for each lesson or assessment. The only required link change on each duplicate is the item’s correct Goblins student link.

Independent Practice One after every numbered lesson. Each duplicate needs its own correct student link; the class code can already be stored in the master.
Concept Check One near the middle of most modules, placed exactly where shown in the tables below.
Summative Assessment One at the end of every module, after the final numbered lesson.

Planning-table assessment rule

Modules with more than three numbered lessons receive one concept check near the midpoint. Every module receives a summative assessment at the end.

Three short-module exceptions have no separate concept check: Grade 3 Module 7, Grade 4 Module 9, and Grade 4 Module 17. Follow the placement tables rather than adding an extra assessment to these modules.

Use a “customize once, duplicate many” workflow

Complete the class-wide setup one time before building individual lesson pages. After that, each lesson or assessment requires only a duplicate, the correct item title, and its unique student link.

Phase 1: Create class-ready master templates once

Prepare one master for Independent Practice, one for Concept Checks, and one for Summative Assessments. Keep these master pages unpublished and clearly labeled so they are never assigned directly to students.

1

Make a working copy of each original template

Duplicate the original Goblins Assignment, Goblins Concept Check, and Goblins Summative Assessment templates. Rename the copies MASTER – Goblins Independent Practice, MASTER – Goblins Concept Check, and MASTER – Goblins Summative Assessment. Leave the original templates untouched as backups.

2

Complete all recurring edits on the masters

Add the teacher name, Canvas Inbox or help directions, class-specific wording, and any other information that will stay the same across the course. Replace the visible 000-000 with the class’s six-digit code. Keep the hyphen.

Example Class Code 016-405
3

Finish and protect the master templates

Remove the gray Teacher Setup box and resolve every recurring EDIT ME field. Do not add an assignment student link yet. Leave the green button’s placeholder URL in the master. Save the masters, keep them unpublished, and place them in a clearly labeled teacher-only area if your course design allows.

Phase 2: Duplicate the correct master for each item

The class code, teacher information, and standard directions will already be complete. Teachers should not rebuild or re-customize the page for every lesson.

4

Duplicate, rename, and place the page

Duplicate the matching master. Rename the new Canvas page to match the lesson or assessment code in the planning table. Update only item-specific text that must change, such as the visible assignment title or learning target, then place the page in the location shown in the scope-and-sequence tables below.

Add only that item’s Goblins student link

Create or assign the correct item in Goblins and copy its student link. Do not copy a teacher-dashboard or editing link. In the duplicated Canvas page’s HTML, replace only the URL inside the green button’s href="...".

Before: <a href="https://gob.live" ...>
After:  <a href="PASTE-THIS-ITEMS-STUDENT-LINK-HERE" ...>

Leave the button style, target, class code, teacher information, and all other recurring content unchanged.

6

Test and publish the duplicate

Use Student View or another student-safe test. Confirm that the green button opens the intended Goblins student page and that the master’s class code remains correct. Verify the page title and Canvas-module placement, then publish the duplicate. Never publish the master template itself.

Before publishing each page

  • The page was duplicated from the correct class-ready master; the master itself remains unpublished.
  • The Canvas page title matches the lesson or assessment code in the planning table.
  • The green button opens the correct student link—not the teacher dashboard.
  • The six-digit class code is correct and includes the hyphen.
  • No placeholder text such as EDIT ME or 000-000 remains.
  • The gray Teacher Setup box has been removed.
  • The item appears in the correct position in the Canvas module.

New Student Guide

Welcome to Goblins!

Meet your one-on-one math helper. You will show your thinking, explain your ideas, and get support right when you need it.

Teacher Setup — delete this box before publishing

In the HTML editor, search for EDIT ME. Add your direct Goblins assignment link, class code, teacher name, completion directions, and help link. A direct assignment link gives students the simplest experience.

💡

What is Goblins?

Goblins is an AI-powered math tutor that works alongside your teacher. It watches the math work you choose to share and listens when you explain your reasoning. If you get stuck, it asks helpful questions, draws models, or gives a short mini-lesson. Its job is to help you understand the math—not simply hand you an answer.

🛡️

Use AI with character

Your Goblins conversations and math sessions are monitored and may be reviewed by your teachers. Your teacher can look at your explanations, written work, and conversations to understand how you are thinking and how to help you grow.

Practice responsibility, self-government, and courtesy whenever you speak, draw, or type—even when you are talking with AI. Stay focused on the assignment, use respectful school-appropriate language, and communicate as thoughtfully as you would with a teacher or classmate.

Show your thinking your way

🎙️

Speak

Explain what you notice and why you chose each step.

✏️

Draw

Write equations, label models, and show your work on the math canvas.

⌨️

Type

Type an explanation when speaking or drawing is not the best choice.

Before your first visit

  1. Use a laptop or Chromebook with a reliable internet connection.
  2. Have paper and a pencil nearby if your teacher asks you to use them.
  3. When your browser asks for microphone permission, select Allow if you plan to explain your thinking aloud.
  4. Enter the name or school sign-in your teacher has told you to use. Do not create a second student profile.

How to open your assignment

Always begin on the Canvas page for the lesson you are completing. That page will send you to the correct Goblins work.

1
Click the green Goblins button on your Canvas lesson or assignment page.
2
Sign in only if asked. First-time students may also need the class code shown below.
3
Check the assignment name. It should match the name listed in Canvas. If it does not match, return to Canvas instead of starting a different assignment.
4
Complete every problem and follow the Canvas directions for reporting that you are finished.
Open Goblins in a New Tab
Class code, if requested [EDIT ME: CLASS CODE]

When Goblins asks you a question…

Pause and think before responding. Goblins may ask you to explain a step, try a smaller example, or look at a model. That does not mean you failed—it means the tutor is helping you build the idea.

A strong response sounds like: “I multiplied here because…,” “I notice that…,” “My model shows…,” or “I am confused about this step because…”

When you finish

I do not see the correct assignment
Return to the Canvas lesson and open the Goblins link again. Check the assignment title carefully. If it is still missing, contact your teacher; do not complete a different assignment.
My microphone is not working
Check the microphone symbol near the browser address bar and allow microphone access. Make sure the correct microphone is selected. You may type or draw your thinking while you wait for help.
The page is frozen or will not load
Refresh the page once. If that does not work, close the Goblins tab, return to Canvas, and reopen the assignment link. Check your internet connection before trying again.
